title: Hong Kong gold hub, quantum crypto risk, and overdue STR quality fixes
summary: Hong Kong's 2027 gold clearing platform raises fresh AML typology questions; Google's Willow quantum chip tightens the timeline on crypto key vulnerability; and HKMA's STR quality thematic findings are still open for a quarter of supervised institutions. What to do about all three.
script:
ALEX: The news today is genuinely thin, and I want to use that as an opportunity rather than a problem. Three items, each at a different stage of the compliance lifecycle. One is structural and coming fast, one is technical and often dismissed, and one is overdue and sitting on desks right now. Jordan, which one worries you most this Monday morning?

JORDAN: The overdue one, always. But let's take them in the order that builds the argument, because I think they actually connect.

ALEX: Agreed. Start with Hong Kong and gold. The government has confirmed it will launch a centralised gold clearing platform in the first quarter of 2027. That is roughly fifteen months away. The pitch is that Hong Kong can differentiate itself from London as a primary bullion trading hub, and the infrastructure is now moving from aspiration to operational planning. For an AML supervisor, the question is immediate: what is the AML framework for this platform, and who owns it?

JORDAN: Right, and here is where I want to push on the framing slightly. The government announcement focuses on market infrastructure, on clearing mechanics, on positioning Hong Kong as a credible rival to the London Bullion Market Association. What it does not foreground is that gold has a well-documented role in trade-based money laundering, in sanctions evasion, and in the movement of value across borders with minimal documentary trail. The Joint Financial Intelligence Unit published typologies on this years ago and they remain current.

ALEX: So what is the supervisory read? My instinct is that the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission will need to issue guidance on the AML obligations that attach to participants in this clearing platform before it goes live. The question is whether fifteen months is enough runway for that guidance to be written, consulted on, and absorbed by firms.

JORDAN: I think it probably is enough time, if they start now. And that is actually the action item for any institution that is positioning for participation in this platform. Do not wait for the guidance. Map your existing customer due diligence and transaction monitoring frameworks against the gold sector typologies today. FATF Recommendation 22 applies to dealers in precious metals, and if your institution is going to clear bullion trades, you need to understand whether your current controls cover that activity or whether you have a gap that needs remediation before Q1 2027.

ALEX: On that point I agree. Moving on. The second item is Google's Willow quantum processor, and the updated assessment of what it means for cryptographically vulnerable bitcoin holdings, specifically the coins locked in early pay-to-public-key outputs from the Satoshi era. The headline is that Willow has materially narrowed the theoretical timeline within which those outputs could be compromised. I want to be precise about "narrowed," because I have seen this story overstated.

JORDAN: Yes, and I want to push back on the dismissiveness I hear from compliance teams when this topic comes up. The standard response is "quantum is decades away, this is not my problem today." But that is the wrong frame for a regulated firm.

ALEX: How so?

JORDAN: Because your obligation is not to wait until the attack is possible and then respond. Your obligation is to assess the risk now and document your assessment. If you are a virtual asset service provider, or a bank with a crypto custody business, your AML and technology risk frameworks should already include a section on quantum vulnerability. Not because the attack is imminent, but because regulators will ask whether you have considered it, and "we assumed it was too far away" is not a satisfactory answer to an examiner.

ALEX: I take that point, but I want to add a layer. The more immediate money laundering risk from quantum developments is not the breaking of existing bitcoin keys. It is the market behaviour that follows the news cycle. Every time a credible quantum milestone is reported, you see movement in older dormant wallets, holders trying to migrate assets to quantum-resistant address formats. That movement creates transaction monitoring noise and, potentially, a typology question about why specific wallets are moving after years of inactivity.

JORDAN: That is a fair point and it connects directly to episode two of this week, where we talked about dormant wallet movement. The transaction monitoring read-across is real. If your VASP's monitoring rules do not flag sudden activity on wallets dormant for more than, say, three years, that is a tuning gap worth reviewing this week.

ALEX: Agreed. And now to the item that I suspect is most immediately actionable for the majority of our listeners in Hong Kong. The HKMA's STR quality thematic review from the fourth quarter of 2025 is still open. Deficiency letters went to approximately twenty-five percent of the authorised institution population in early 2026. We are now in October 2026. Those findings are still unresolved for a significant number of firms.

JORDAN: And this is where I will be direct with any MLRO listening who is in that cohort. If you received a deficiency letter and have not closed the findings, your position is deteriorating, not stabilising. The HKMA's Section 11 annual self-assessment return under the HKMA AML and CFT Guideline was due at the end of September. If you submitted that return while your STR quality thematic findings were still open, the examiner reading your return will see the gap immediately.

ALEX: The obligation under the HKMA SPM CG-5 framework is clear. The thematic findings require a formal closure response, and the quality of that response will be part of your supervisory relationship going into the next examination cycle. What should listeners actually do?

JORDAN: Three things. The first is to pull your deficiency letter this week and map every finding to a named owner and a closure date. If you do not have that mapping, you are not managing the remediation, you are just hoping it closes. The second is to review the STR narratives you have filed since the thematic review was issued. The HKMA's concern was narrative quality, so check whether your narratives actually explain the basis for suspicion in the specific, fact-grounded way the guideline requires, or whether they are still formulaic. The third is to ensure that your board or risk committee has visibility on the open findings. Under Section 16 of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, governance accountability sits at the top. If your board does not know you have open thematic findings, that is a governance gap on top of the original quality gap.

ALEX: And for Australian listeners, your annual AML and CTF Program review under Section 84 of the AML and CTF Act has a board-level approval requirement. If that review and approval has not been completed and documented, the fourth quarter is when examiners start asking. Get it on the board agenda now, not in December.

JORDAN: Before we close, the through-line today is timing. The gold platform is fifteen months out, which sounds comfortable until you remember how long it takes to get AML guidance written, absorbed, and built into controls. Quantum risk is easy to defer and easy to dismiss, but the transaction monitoring implication is live right now. And the STR quality findings are already overdue. All three reward the firms that move early.

ALEX: If any of that felt uncomfortably close to your Monday morning inbox, that is exactly what this briefing is for. Full obligation register and source links are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. We will be back tomorrow.
